title: The Missing Signal
intro: An AI assistant helped write a workshop announcement for the village noticeboard. Some of the details may be wrong. Check them before anyone sees it.

objectives.label: Tell an original source apart from an AI-generated summary
Spot where two pieces of information disagree
Choose a sensible way to check a claim before using it
Explain why a prompt needs context and limits

evidence.title: Organiser's notice
body: Beginner Tech Workshop: Getting Started with Online Tools
This Saturday, 14:00–16:00, Willowmere Community Hall, Room 2.
A small number of laptops (10) are available to borrow.
Please register at the library desk so we can plan seats.

evidence.title: Assistant's summary
evidence.from: An AI writing assistant, asked to "summarise the workshop"
body: Join us for an exciting Tech Workshop this Saturday at 15:00 at Willowmere Community Hall!
No registration needed. Just turn up!

evidence.title: Message from Tobin
body: Someone told me the workshop starts at 3 now? Not totally sure though.

badge.name: Signal Restorer
badge.description: Checked an AI-written announcement against its source before publishing.

takeaway: AI can save you time drafting, but it can also state wrong details confidently. Before you share something important, compare it with the original source.

scenes.title: The village noticeboard
scenes.speaker: mira
lines: Pathfinder, you came! The noticeboard signal has gone quiet, and we need it working before the workshop.
An AI assistant drafted the announcement for us. It reads well, but I'm not sure every detail is right.
Will you help me check it before we publish?

scenes.title: Gather the evidence
scenes.speaker: mira
lines: Here's everything I have. Open each item and read it carefully. Notice where each one came from.

scenes.title: Find the source
scenes.speaker: mira
scenes.context: Before we compare details, we need to know which document to trust most.
scenes.prompt: Which piece of evidence is the original source of the workshop details?

options.feedback: Yes. The library is running the workshop, so its notice is where the details come from.
The summary was made from other information. It's a copy, not the source, and copies can pick up mistakes.
Tobin is passing on something he heard. He even says he isn't sure, so it's second-hand at best.

options.text: None of them. They're all equally reliable
options.feedback: They aren't equal. One came from the people running the event. The others are retellings.

hints: Look at the "From" line on each card. Who is actually organising the workshop?
A source is where information starts. Summaries and messages repeat it.
scenes.explanation: An original source comes from the person or organisation responsible for the information. Summaries, including AI summaries, are retellings and can introduce errors.

scenes.title: Spot the conflict
scenes.speaker: mira
scenes.context: Let's compare the first lines of the organiser's notice and the AI draft.
scenes.prompt: Compare the day, start time and place. Which of these does not match?

options.feedback: Both say "this Saturday", so the day matches.
Well spotted. The notice says 14:00 but the AI draft says 15:00.
Both mention Willowmere Community Hall. The draft leaves out the room number, but it doesn't contradict the notice.
Look again at the numbers. One detail is different between the two.

hints: Read the times in each document side by side.
The notice says 14:00. What time does the AI draft give?
scenes.explanation: A contradiction is when two sources give different answers to the same question. Here the start time differs, so at least one of them is wrong.

scenes.title: Decide what to do
scenes.speaker: mira
scenes.context: The notice says the workshop begins at 14:00. The AI summary says 15:00.
scenes.prompt: What should you do before publishing the announcement?

options.text: Trust the AI because it sounds confident
options.feedback: A confident tone isn't proof. AI tools can state wrong details just as smoothly as right ones.

options.text: Choose whichever time looks more reasonable
options.feedback: Both times look reasonable, and that's the problem. Guessing doesn't tell you which is true.

options.text: Check the original notice and use the verified time
options.feedback: Exactly. The notice comes from the organiser, so 14:00 is the time you can stand behind.
That would give 14:30, a time nobody announced. Combining two answers doesn't make either one correct.

hints: Which document did you decide was the original source?
When two versions disagree, go back to where the information started.
scenes.explanation: Fluent, confident language is not proof of accuracy. When an AI output and a source disagree, go with the source, or ask the source directly.

scenes.title: A second opinion?
scenes.speaker: mira
scenes.context: Tobin's message also says the workshop starts "at 3". So now two things say 15:00.
scenes.prompt: Does Tobin's message mean you should publish 15:00?

options.text: Yes. Two sources say 15:00, so it must be right
options.feedback: Counting votes doesn't work here. Tobin may have heard the time from someone who read the AI draft, so it could be the same mistake repeated.

options.text: No. Keep 14:00 unless the organiser confirms a change
options.feedback: Right. A rumour isn't confirmation. If the time really changed, the organiser can tell you. Until then, use the source.

options.text: Publish both times so people can choose
options.feedback: Two times would confuse people and some would miss the start. An announcement should give one verified time.
You don't need to give up. You already have a reliable source. Publish what it says.

hints: Where might Tobin have heard "3 o'clock"? Could it trace back to the AI draft?
Is a message that says "not totally sure" the same as confirmation from the organiser?
scenes.explanation: Repeating a claim doesn't make it more true. Information that spreads from one mistaken source can look like agreement. Ask who actually knows, and check with them.

scenes.title: Improve the instructions
scenes.speaker: mira
scenes.context: Mira wants to ask the AI assistant for a new draft. The first attempt only said: "Write something about the workshop."
scenes.prompt: Which prompt is most likely to get an accurate, useful draft?

options.feedback: This is the original prompt. It gives no facts, no audience and no format, so the assistant fills the gaps by guessing.

options.text: "Write an exciting announcement about the workshop and make it sound amazing."
options.feedback: Asking for excitement without facts encourages exaggeration, like promising free laptops for everyone.

options.text: "Using only the organiser's notice below, write a 60-word announcement for local beginners. Include the time, place, cost and how to register. If a detail is missing, say so instead of guessing."
options.feedback: Yes. It gives the source, the audience, the length, what to include, and tells the assistant not to make things up.

options.text: "Write the announcement and fix any mistakes yourself."
options.feedback: The assistant has no way to know what's correct without the source. It can't check facts it was never given.

hints: A good prompt tells the assistant what information to use, who it's for, and what form you want.
Look for the prompt that hands over the source and says what to do when something is missing.
scenes.explanation: Useful prompts share purpose, source material and limits. Even with a good prompt, you still need to check the result, because it can still contain errors.

scenes.title: Build the final announcement
scenes.speaker: mira
scenes.context: Now put the announcement together. Use only details the organiser's notice supports.
scenes.prompt: Choose one option for each line, then tick any extra details you want to include.
scenes.heading: Beginner Tech Workshop
scenes.successFeedback: Every line matches the organiser's notice.

options.feedback: 15:00 came from the AI draft. The organiser's notice says 14:00.
14:30 doesn't appear anywhere. It's a guess between two times.
The notice says only 10 laptops are available to borrow, not one for everyone. Free to keep is never mentioned.

options.text: A small number of laptops are available to borrow
You must bring your own laptop
options.feedback: The notice doesn't say laptops are required. It offers some to borrow.

options.text: No registration needed, just turn up
options.feedback: The notice asks people to register at the library desk. "No registration" was invented by the AI draft.

options.text: Please register at the library desk

options.feedback: Nothing in the notice mentions online registration.

extras.feedback: Lunch isn't mentioned in the notice. Leave out details you can't support.
A certificate isn't mentioned in the notice. It sounds nice, but it's unsupported.

hints: Keep the organiser's notice open and check each line against it.
Anything that only appears in the AI draft, or nowhere at all, should be left out.
scenes.explanation: Every line now matches the organiser's notice, and nothing unsupported was added. That is an announcement you can publish with confidence.

scenes.title: The signal returns
scenes.speaker: mira
lines: It's live! The noticeboard is glowing again, and every detail matches the organiser's notice.
The AI helped us start the draft, but you made sure it was true. That part is always our job.
Look at the map. Paths are opening beyond the woods.
